title: Understanding Florida Probate Rules (November 2026)
summary: Understand when Florida probate is required and what the process involves, as of November 2026.
body_markdown:
During estate settlement in Florida, assets held solely in the deceased's name generally go through[probate](https://www.elayne.com/resources/probate-explained-what-happens-after-someone-dies-and-how-to-plan-ahead) , a court-supervised process. Whether probate is needed depends on how each asset is owned and whether it can transfer directly to a beneficiary. This guide explains key points for families and personal representatives to be aware of, including: when probate is required, which assets are covered, three types of administration, how the formal process works, and more.


**Key Takeaways:**


- Florida probate generally applies to sole-name assets with no transfer outside probate.
- Will custodians must deposit the will with the court within 10 days of learning of the death.
- Formal probate usually takes 6 to 12 months and generally requires a Florida attorney.
- Elayne organizes estate records and uses Verified Asset Search to find overlooked accounts.


## What Probate Is


Probate is the court-supervised process of gathering a deceased person’s assets, paying valid debts, and transferring remaining property to beneficiaries or heirs.


{{blog-cta-financial}}


## When Probate Is Required in Florida


Probate is generally required[in Florida](https://www.elayne.com/resources/florida-probate-process-timeline) when someone dies owning assets solely in their name without a valid beneficiary designation or another arrangement for transfer outside probate. A will does not, by itself, avoid probate. The will names who receives property that passes through probate, and it takes effect as to that property only after the court admits the will to probate.


## Assets That Generally Require Probate vs. Assets That Generally Do Not


Generally require probate Generally bypass probate


Individually owned real estate Survivorship property


Bank accounts without beneficiaries Payable-on-death accounts


Investments without transfer-on-death instructions Transfer-on-death investments


Vehicles without transfer arrangements; business interests Trust-held assets


Life insurance payable to estate Insurance with named beneficiaries


Florida’s exempt property protections shield qualifying property from estate creditors for eligible family members. Exemption from creditor claims differs from bypassing probate through ownership or beneficiary arrangements.


## Three Types of Florida Probate Administration


**Formal administration** is the full court-supervised process.


**Summary administration** is available for qualifying estates, including those where the death occurred more than two years ago.


**Disposition without administration** applies to limited, qualifying personal-property estates.


Florida's updated estate limits, effective July 1, 2026:


Procedure Previous limit Updated limit


Summary administration: nonexempt assets $75,000 $150,000


Disposition without administration: qualifying intestate personal-property estates $10,000 $20,000


The[Florida Senate estate bill analysis](https://www.flsenate.gov/Session/Bill/2026/1500/Analyses/2026s01500.pre.rc.PDF) describes these increases. Disposition without administration requires more than meeting the value limit.


**Historical example only: the $75,000 summary-administration limit before July 1, 2026:**


- Hypothetical estate value subject to administration: $75,000.
- Exempt property: none in this example.
- Applicable value limit: $75,000 under the earlier rule described in the analysis.
- Time condition: the death occurred less than two years ago, so the separate time-based eligibility route does not apply.
- Consequence: the estate meets the value condition for summary administration, subject to the other legal requirements.


Meeting a value limit can make a shorter court procedure available; it does not mean probate is unnecessary.


## Probate With a Will vs. Probate Without a Will in Florida


- With a will, the named executor petitions for appointment. The custodian must deposit the will with the court within 10 days of learning of the death.
- Without a will,[Florida intestate succession](https://www.elayne.com/resources/florida-intestate-succession-laws) law determines inheritance.[Appointment priority](https://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0700-0799/0733/Sections/0733.301.html) generally follows: surviving spouse, heirs’ majority-in-interest choice, then nearest eligible heir.


## Duties of the Personal Representative


Once appointed, the personal representative receives Letters of Administration. Their role includes:


- Inventorying assets and protecting estate property.
- Notifying creditors and beneficiaries.
- Paying valid debts and applicable taxes.
- Distributing remaining assets to those entitled to inherit.


The representative has legal responsibilities called fiduciary duties, including treating beneficiaries impartially and keeping careful records.


## The Formal Administration Process


1. A petition is filed with the circuit court in the deceased’s county of domicile. An interested person, usually through an attorney, requests that the estate be opened and a personal representative appointed. Filing the petition alone does not confer authority to manage estate assets.
2. The court appoints a personal representative; beneficiaries and creditors receive notice. Letters of Administration document the representative’s authority to act for the estate. The representative, generally assisted by an attorney, is responsible for arranging the required notices.
3. The publication-based creditor claim period starts at first publication of the Notice to Creditors, not when the petition is filed. Known or reasonably ascertainable creditors generally receive direct notice, which can affect their filing deadlines. The personal representative reviews filed claims with the attorney while other estate work continues.
4. Assets are inventoried and appraised as needed. The personal representative prepares an inventory identifying estate assets and their estimated fair market values at the date of death. Account statements can support financial-asset values, while qualified appraisers may be engaged to value real estate, business interests, or other property requiring specialist assessment.
5. Valid claims and taxes are paid before remaining assets are distributed. The personal representative uses estate funds to pay these obligations and administration expenses, following statutory priority. Disputed claims and unresolved tax obligations can delay final distribution.
6. Final accounting and discharge procedures close the estate. Unless properly waived, the personal representative provides a final accounting showing estate receipts, payments, distributions, and property remaining for distribution. After required distributions and closing requirements are completed, the court enters an order of discharge ending the representative’s appointment.

## How Elayne Supports Families Settling Florida Estates


[Elayne](https://www.elayne.com/company) is an online service for the records, accounts, and deadlines involved in settling an estate. Elayne's support is organized into three cumulative steps, each including the one before it:


- **Estate Organizer** gathers documents, contacts, and accounts into one estate record and prepares the family for probate or a conversation with an attorney. County-specific probate guides describe the court process where the estate is administered, from the petition through the order of discharge.
- **Financial Discovery** adds Verified Asset Search, which looks for real property, vehicles, life insurance, unclaimed property, and accounts that sole-name paperwork may not reveal. A credit-bureau search also locates debts reported by Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion, which bear on the creditor claims an estate may face. Document analysis of tax returns and bank statements can point to institutions holding estate assets.
- **Inheritance Plan** maps who inherits and how each asset transfers. Assets are sorted into categories such as probate, trust, joint ownership, and beneficiary designation, which mirrors the division between probate and non-probate property in Florida. Date-of-death account values, EIN application support, and help opening an estate bank account are part of this step.


Across all steps, Elayne also:


- Cancels subscriptions and recurring charges directly with providers, monitors later statements to confirm the charges stopped, and logs each confirmation for estate accounting.
- Identifies survivor benefits that may apply, including Social Security, pension, veterans', and union benefits, along with the eligibility requirements and deadlines attached to each.
- Locates newspapers that qualify for Notice to Creditors publication in the Florida county where the estate is administered, tracks the publication timeline, and flags when proof of publication is due to the court.
- Tracks inherited-retirement-account distribution deadlines and required minimum distributions, which vary by account and beneficiary circumstances as explained in[IRS beneficiary guidance](https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/plan-participant-employee/retirement-topics-beneficiary) .
- Gives co-executors and family members a shared dashboard with role-based permissions, document sharing, and progress tracking, so everyone with authorized access works from the same record.
- Guides families through posthumous credit freezes and identity theft protection.


Elayne is designed to work alongside attorneys. Florida formal administration, Probate Rule 5.030 generally requires a personal representative to be represented by a Florida-licensed attorney, who handles the court filings. Elayne's organized estate record gives a family's attorney a documented overview of assets, beneficiaries, and open questions at the start of the matter. Attorneys can access documents, account records, and progress tracking through the same shared dashboard as family members.


## FAQ


### Can Elayne help locate life insurance policies that may be missing from a Florida estate?


Yes. Elayne’s Verified Asset Search can help locate potentially overlooked life insurance policies, though results vary by estate and access depends on verified authority. A policy payable to a named beneficiary generally bypasses probate, while one payable to the estate generally becomes part of the probate estate.


### How is a Florida probate property list prepared with Elayne when some assets have beneficiaries?


The list separates potential probate assets from assets with documented beneficiary or survivorship arrangements. For each asset, useful records include ownership details, beneficiary information, date-of-death value, and supporting statements or deeds; Elayne helps organize those records. Keeping uncertain ownership or beneficiary details marked for review helps the estate's attorney identify what still needs confirmation.


### Who is qualified to serve as a personal representative in Florida?


The court decides who is appointed. Under[Florida Statutes § 733.303](https://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0700-0799/0733/Sections/0733.303.html) , a person is not qualified if convicted of a felony, convicted of abuse, neglect, or exploitation of an elderly person or disabled adult, mentally or physically unable to perform the duties, or under the age of 18.


A person who is not domiciled in Florida qualifies only if related to the deceased in a listed way, such as a spouse, adopted child, lineal relative, sibling, uncle, aunt, nephew, or niece, as set out in[Section 733.304](https://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0700-0799/0733/Sections/0733.304.html) . If the person named in a will is not qualified, the court grants letters under the statutory order of priority.
